summary:
Bahia is a state in north-east Brazil and stands under the national framework described above: the federal constitutional and criminal prohibitions on SOGI discrimination, the 2018 removal of the surgical requirement for legal gender change, equal age of consent, same-sex marriage and spousal-visa equality, and National Council of Justice Resolution 348/366 governing the placement of LGBTI detainees all extend to Bahia and to its prison system.

Bahia records one of the country's highest burdens of trans and travesti killings. The ANTRA 2025 dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, counts 7 trans people killed in Bahia during 2025, behind only the states recording 8; on the same national reckoning, which counts 1,261 killings across Brazil from 2017 to 2025, Bahia ranks third with 97, after São Paulo at 151 and Ceará at 107. Valor Internacional recorded the same state-level counts on 27 January 2026, placing Bahia behind the Ceará and Minas Gerais pair.

The figure is persistent rather than a single-year outlier. The ANTRA dossier for 2022 ranked Bahia seventh among the Brazilian states, with 7 killings of travestis recorded in the state that year, putting Bahia in the top band of consecutive annual dossiers.

Individual cases show how the violence is charged and processed. On the weekend of 6–7 December 2025, Rhianna, an 18-year-old trans woman, was choked to death in Luís Eduardo Magalhães, in the west of Bahia. The suspect, a 19-year-old app driver, drove the victim's body to the police station himself, confessed, and claimed self-defence; he was released. The Civil Police confirmed that the case is being investigated as a feminicide, and the state police framed the killing as gender-based, so the killing of a trans woman in Bahia was classified as gender-based violence while the accused was initially set free.

For a trans visitor, the practical exposure is the violence risk and its investigative handling rather than any entry, document or visa rule: the national framework applies Bahia's entry and family-law treatment on the same footing as for anyone else, and no Bahia-specific rule governing where trans detainees are held was located in the sources reviewed.
tangentialFactors:
Bahia's ranking sits within a national total of 1,261 trans killings recorded across Brazil from 2017 to 2025, so the state-level figures are part of a countrywide pattern rather than an isolated local one. The national counts have fallen over the last two years, according to Valor Internacional's reporting of 27 January 2026, while Bahia remains in the highest-burden group.

Outside the prison context, the national framework supplies the remedies a visitor or resident would rely on: the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling places transphobia on the same footing as racism, and lower courts have pressed the Superior Court of Justice toward extending the Maria da Penha Law and Feminicide Law to trans women. The Luís Eduardo Magalhães investigation is an instance of the feminicide charge being applied to a trans victim in Bahia.
localsOnly:
The national rules on detention apply inside Bahia's prison system: National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, requires a judge to fix a detainee's place of deprivation of liberty in a reasoned decision after consulting them, listing the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and asking trans, travesti and intersex people which they prefer, with LGBTI-specific spaces barred from use as disciplinary isolation and compulsory transfer as punishment prohibited. LGBTI status for these purposes is established by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing.

Brazilian prisoners are documented as having a special, separate place in prisons, the right to be addressed by their social name rather than their birth name, the right to be forwarded to women's prisons, and the right to choose male or female clothing; same-sex-partner conjugal visitations have been available in all Brazilian jails since February 2015 under the National Criminal and Penitentiary Council. These are national provisions applying in Bahia.

Local killings are investigated by the Bahia Civil Police, which confirmed the feminicide investigation in Luís Eduardo Magalhães, and the state police's framing of the case as gender-based.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Bahia-specific prison placement rule, special unit, segregation practice, or documented case of a trans prisoner's housing in the state was found in the sources reviewed. The Bahia prison administration (Secretaria de Administração Penitenciária da Bahia) issues no placement detail in the material available, so how Resolution 348/366 is applied inside Bahia's own units, and whether practice there follows the Rio de Janeiro pattern of housing trans women in masculine units documented in the 2021 census, remain unresolved and not sourced.

The source inventory contains no entry-, visa- or document-screening account specific to Bahia, and no account of trans-specific facilities, healthcare access or partner recognition in the state; the national framework is taken to govern these, but state-level implementation is unverified here. The count of killings for 2025 and the cumulative 2017–2025 figures derive from ANTRA dossiers as reported by third-party outlets rather than from a primary state record.
